title: Shemini: Aaron's silence (Leviticus 10:3)
hookLine: after his sons die, "Aaron held his peace"

lines: THE GREAT DAY, AND TWO SONS GONE.
cards: A visit to a house of mourning often has a moment at the door: a sentence rehearsed in the car, then the person's face, and every prepared word sounds wrong.

It's tempting to talk anyway, because silence can feel like failure. Leviticus has a scene like that, only the one who can't find words is the father. On the great day of dedication, fire consumed Aaron's two eldest sons.
Moses turns to his brother with a hard theological sentence. And the Torah gives Aaron's answer in two Hebrew words, which say only that he was still.

teach.b: Start with what Moses said. The Lord had spoken, he tells Aaron, of being sanctified through those who are near.
Rashi hears Moses trying to comfort: I knew this house would be made holy through someone close to God; I thought it would be you or me; now I see your sons were greater than us both.
Then, what Aaron did: "And Aaron held his peace." In Hebrew, vayidom Aharon. The verb means to be still; a psalm uses the same word for being still before God and waiting.
It isn't described as calm. It's described as quiet. Rashi notes that Aaron was rewarded for that silence: a few verses later, God speaks to Aaron directly, without Moses in between.
Commentators have read the silence many ways: acceptance, shock, a grief too big for speech, even a protest held back.

teach.h: A SILENCE THE TEXT DOESN'T EXPLAIN.
teach.b: The text doesn't say which. And it shaped how mourners are visited.

teach.h: AT SHIVA, THE MOURNER SPEAKS FIRST.
teach.b: Jewish law teaches that visitors to a house of shiva wait for the mourner to speak first.
In the book of Job, before the long speeches begin, his friends sit with him seven days and seven nights, and none of them says a word. A closed mouth and a chair pulled close can be the whole visit.

how: When Jews visit a house of mourning during shiva, the seven days after a burial, custom holds that visitors sit quietly and wait for the mourner to speak first, and the conversation follows the mourner's lead.

o: eighth: the portion of the first service day
mourning: the seven days after a loss
stillness: what Aaron did after the fire

games.q: what's inside the silence — tap the pairs.
p: near ones make God's name holy
sat seven days without a word

s: the text tells us exactly what Aaron felt
it says only that he held his peace. commentators read it as acceptance, shock or grief; the text is silent.
at shiva, custom says the mourner speaks first
visitors wait for the mourner to open the conversation.
he said nothing at all: vayidom Aharon.

games.q: you're Aaron. your two sons have just died, and your brother has offered you a theological explanation. what do you do?
games.why: Aaron held his peace. Rashi says he was rewarded: soon after, God speaks to Aaron alone.

practice: Bring to mind someone in your life who is carrying a loss, and keep them company in your mind, without planning what to say and without fixing anything.
If no one comes to mind, sit with Aaron at the edge of the camp, and let the quiet be enough.

wordCard.voice: Shemini, the eighth: the portion where the great day turns to grief, and Aaron holds his peace.

orig.note: Hebrew: "and Aaron was still." from the root d-m-m, to be silent, to be still.

carryVoice: Your line: and Aaron held his peace. Sometimes being there is the whole answer. Another week of Leviticus behind you now.
